name: Étain Óg

attributes.attribute: linked to horse goddess Epona, Macha, and Rhiannon
won Étain through a game of fidchell

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Étain Óg is an Irish heroine or goddess. The name also appears as Etaine, Aideen, Édain, Edain, and Achtan. Many Irish figures bear this name, so they are often confused. Their myths use reincarnation, disguise, and false identity. They all may descend from one common goddess, perhaps a sun goddess. The name means 'swift one'. The old title Echraide means 'horse-rider'. These join her to horse goddesses such as Epona, Rhiannon, and Macha. The Celts tied the horse to the sun, a steed none could outrun. One myth makes Étain the lover of Midir. Midir was a fairy king of the Otherworld. His wife Fuamnach held the powers of a druid and sorceress. She turned Étain into a fly. For long years she flew through the world in that shape. At last she dropped into wine that an Ulster princess held. The princess swallowed the fly with the drink and grew pregnant. She bore a girl, also named Étain, who became the most noted woman in Ireland. Eochaid Airem sought the kingship at Tara. He could not hold his inauguration until he married. The rite needed a queen to play the land goddess. He found the fair Étain, who had forgot her earlier life. She consented to be his wife. Their wedding and his inauguration passed in high order. Then all seemed set for a happy future. Midir did not forget Étain. He came to Tara as Ailill, a feigned illness. He said only Étain's touch could soothe him. Étain agreed to accept him to save a life. Most versions have her reject him in the end. Midir then challenged Eochaid to Fidchell, a game like cribbage. He wagered and won Étain as the prize.

okr.objective: Étain Óg is the Irish sun goddess and heroine of many myths.
key_results: She links to the horse goddess Epona, Rhiannon, and Macha.
Fuamnach turned the fly that became her.
